doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: 'Sinister Minister', 'Big Country' and the band name
summary: Howard Levy suggested 'Sinister Minister' as a funny title. A good title connects with listeners, and Fleck wonders whether the Flecktones name made some take them less seriously.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: Is there a story behind “Sinister Minister?”
Not really. We were just looking for a title and I think Howard Levy came up with it and we all thought that was funny. And anytime someone had a title that made us laugh we tried to use it.
Okay. The titles can put a spin on things that may not be your intention.

Yeah. But it seemed to fit the song perfectly. It made the song more than what the song was before it had that title. I don’t know how. I don’t know why. It worked that way with “Sunset Road” too. And I think “Big Country.” Sometimes when you get a really classic title for a song the song has that much more — there’s another connection for the listener. It’s not, “oh what’s that song, cut eleven on whatever record, I like that song whatever that was.” It’s like “I like ‘Big Country.’ I like ‘Sinister Minister.’” It’s a connect. So a title is really important. I always wondered whether Béla Fleck and the Flecktones was the best name for the band. It just seemed like the right one at the time and then we were in and it was too late to re-think it. But I think some people think, many people think it was some like California jazz, contemporary jazz thing or something, or like some silly — you know, the graphics and the covers, they made it take us less seriously for some people. But it’s worked out.
